title: Part 6 — Full-stack & deploy
tagline: A REST API, JWT sign-in, React on top, then online for free.
intro: The last part joins it all: an Express backend returning JSON, a React frontend calling it, users signing up and in, and all three running online.
The sample code is a small shop. Follow it once, then rebuild it for an app idea of your own: that is the project for your CV.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Six steps, about four to six weeks.

blocks.caption: From an API on your machine to an app with a live link.

items.label: Design the REST API
items.detail: One path per resource; the method says what to do, the status says how it went
explain: GET /api/products lists, POST /api/products creates, PUT /api/products/7 updates, DELETE /api/products/7 removes. Paths are nouns; the verb is the method.
Return the right code: 201 on create, 400 for bad data, 401 when signed out, 404 when missing. The frontend reads the code to decide what to show.

items.label: Try it in Postman
items.detail: Call the API before any frontend exists, so you know which side a bug is on
explain: Postman sends requests with any method, header and body and shows the response. curl in a terminal does the same.
Save the requests in a Collection: after every backend change, run the set again to make sure nothing broke.

items.label: Connect React to the API
items.detail: React calls the API with fetch; the server enables CORS for the frontend's address
explain: The frontend runs on localhost:5173 and the backend on localhost:3000: a different port is a different origin, so the browser blocks it unless CORS allows it.
The API address lives in VITE_API_URL, so it switches from localhost to the Render link without code changes.

items.label: Sign-in: bcrypt + JWT
items.detail: Store hashed passwords, return a token on sign-in, check it on protected routes
explain: bcrypt.hash turns a password into a string that cannot be reversed; bcrypt.compare checks a typed password against it. The database never holds the real password.
jwt.sign makes a token holding the user id, signed with JWT_SECRET; the requireAuth middleware runs jwt.verify and answers 401 when it is missing or wrong.

items.label: Database to the cloud
items.detail: Free MySQL on Aiven, connected over SSL
explain: Aiven's free plan gives one 1 GB MySQL with no time limit. The tables are created with the same SQL you ran locally in part 5.
Aiven requires SSL: download the CA certificate from the service page and pass it to mysql2 through an environment variable.

items.label: Deploy backend and frontend
items.detail: Backend on Render, frontend on Vercel, both redeploying on every push
explain: Render runs the Node server from the repo's server folder; the Free plan sleeps after 15 idle minutes and takes about a minute to wake.
Vercel builds the client folder with Vite and serves the static files. A vercel.json keeps React Router from returning 404 on reloading a sub-page.

body: Skip lessons #0–#14 of the SERN course: they cover HTML, SCSS and Git, already done in earlier parts.
The course's React part uses React 17, class components and Redux connect, unlike part 4's hooks. Watch it for the data flow; write your own app with hooks as below.

items: Create a my-shop folder and run git init in it.
Create the client with npm create vite@latest client -- --template react.
Copy part 5's shop-api project in as the server folder.
Create a root .gitignore with node_modules, .env and dist, then make the first commit.

sections.title: Designing the REST API
sections.summary: Five routes per resource, enough for any CRUD screen.

blocks.caption: server/server.js: CORS, JSON, routes, a 404 and one error handler.
Install this part's libraries, in the server folder.

sections.title: Trying the API in Postman
sections.summary: Know the API works before writing any React.

items: Install Postman from postman.com/downloads, or the Postman extension in VS Code.
Create a GET to localhost:3000/api/products and press Send: a JSON array and status 200 must come back.
Create a POST; in the Body tab choose raw and JSON, type a product, and Send.
Save the requests in a my-shop Collection to rerun after each backend change.

blocks.caption: The same two requests with curl, nothing to install.

sections.summary: A users table, two routes, one middleware.

body: Never store real passwords, never commit JWT_SECRET, and never put sensitive data in a token: anyone holding it can read its contents.
If npm install bcrypt fails to build, use bcryptjs: the same hash and compare functions, in plain JavaScript with nothing to compile.

sections.title: Connecting React to the API
sections.summary: One shared api() function for every call.

items: In server/.env add CLIENT_URL=http://localhost:5173 so CORS lets the frontend in.
In client, create a .env with VITE_API_URL pointing at the backend.
Create client/src/api.js: it attaches the token to the header and throws with the server's message.
Use api() in components: load the list in useEffect, submit the sign-in form and keep the token.
Run two terminals: node --watch --env-file=.env server.js in server, and npm run dev in client.

blocks.caption: client/.env: only variables starting with VITE_ reach React code.
client/src/api.js: one place for the URL, token and errors.
code: const data = res.status === 204 ? null : await res.json().catch(() => null);

blocks.caption: Sign in: keep the token, and later calls send it automatically.

body: Keeping the token in localStorage is the simple way to learn. Real apps often use an httpOnly cookie so stray JavaScript on the page cannot read it.

sections.title: The database on Aiven
sections.summary: Free MySQL with no time limit.

items: Sign up at console.aiven.io and create a project.
Create service → MySQL → choose the Free plan → Create. Wait for the status to turn Running.
On the service's Overview page, copy Host, Port, User, Password and Database, and download the CA certificate (ca.pem).
Create the tables: run schema.sql with the mysql command below, or connect with DBeaver with SSL on.
Update config/db.js to take a port and SSL as below; locally it keeps using your own MySQL because DB_CA_CERT is empty.

blocks.caption: Load the schema into Aiven. Replace HOST, PORT and the database name with yours; enter the password when asked.
server/config/db.js: SSL turns on when DB_CA_CERT is set.

sections.title: Deploying the backend to Render
sections.summary: The Node server online, redeploying on every push.

items: Add engines to server/package.json so Render uses Node 24, then push the repo to GitHub.
Sign in to render.com with GitHub → New → Web Service → pick the my-shop repo.
Root Directory: server · Runtime: Node · Build Command: npm install · Start Command: node server.js · Instance Type: Free.
Under Environment add Aiven's DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, DB_NAME, DB_CA_CERT (the whole ca.pem), JWT_SECRET, and leave CLIENT_URL empty for now.
Press Create Web Service. Once deployed, open the link like your-app.onrender.com/api/products: JSON means the backend runs.

blocks.caption: Add to server/package.json, beside the existing fields.

body: The server must listen on process.env.PORT: Render picks the port. The REST API section's code already does.

sections.title: Deploying the frontend to Vercel
sections.summary: React built into static files, served over HTTPS.

items: Add client/vercel.json below so every path returns index.html for React Router to handle.
Sign in to vercel.com with GitHub → Add New → Project → Import the my-shop repo.
Root Directory: client. The Framework Preset detects Vite: Build Command npm run build, Output Directory dist.
Under Environment Variables add VITE_API_URL = the Render link, such as https://your-app.onrender.com, then press Deploy.
Back on Render, set CLIENT_URL = the Vercel link (such as https://my-shop.vercel.app) and redeploy so CORS lets the frontend in.
Open the Vercel link on a phone, sign up, sign in, add a product: if it works, the path is done.

blocks.caption: client/vercel.json: reloading /products/7 still opens the right page.

body: VITE_ variables are baked in at build time, so changing VITE_API_URL needs a redeploy. Every VITE_ variable is visible in the browser: never put passwords or secret keys there.

sections.title: Free plan limits
sections.summary: Enough for a portfolio; know them up front.

rows: A Node web service, 750 hours a month
Sleeps after 15 idle minutes; the first call takes about a minute
1 GB storage, 1 GB RAM, no time limit
May be powered off when unused for long (with notice); no SLA

body: Limits were read from each service's pages on 11 October 2026 and may change. Check the pricing page again before choosing.

sections.title: Another way: a VPS with Nginx
sections.summary: Running your own Linux server, as in F8's videos.

items: The WSL playlist, lessons 19–28: SSH into a server, point a domain at its IP, install Nginx, free SSL through Cloudflare, deploy React.
The DevOps playlist: package the app with Docker and run Express with a database through Docker Compose.
Worth learning after deploying with Render and Vercel: you see what those services were doing for you.
